Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Presenting problem: New severe headache for 3 days. Onset sudden on waking; continuous with partial relief from ibuprofen (pain described 8/10 down to ~5/10). Pain generalized, stronger over the right eye. Photophobia and intermittent visual phenomena described as “shooting lights.” Nausea without vomiting. No fever, neck stiffness, focal neurological deficits, or recent head trauma. Sleeps reasonably well and headache does not routinely wake from sleep. Occasional stabbing pain when standing up quickly or moving head. Family history of migraine (mother).
- Clinician plan from transcript: Arrange an in-person appointment for full neurological examination and fundoscopy; check blood pressure; consider changing combined oral contraceptive if migraine with aura is confirmed. Doctor offered to prescribe a stronger analgesic to take with food and advised paracetamol may be taken at the same time. Safety-net advice: attend A&E if headache worsens, becomes unbearable, or changes.
- DDx integration (only diagnoses consistent with transcript):
  - Migraine with visual aura — High likelihood
    - Justification: Photophobia and visual phenomena (“shooting lights”), severe disabling headache, partial analgesic response, family history of migraine; no systemic signs of infection or focal deficits.
  - Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — Moderate likelihood
    - Justification: Young woman on combined oral contraceptive pill (prothrombotic risk) with subacute progressive headache and visual symptoms; positional worsening occasionally reported. No focal deficits or papilledema documented yet.
  - Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — Moderate likelihood
    - Justification: Young woman with persistent headache and transient visual symptoms could be consistent with raised intracranial pressure; fundoscopy pending to assess for papilledema. Lack of obesity status and absent classical features noted as opposing evidence.
- Other less likely considerations from DDx (not primary): subarachnoid hemorrhage (low likelihood per DDx) — considered but less consistent with exam and history. No contradiction between transcript and DDx that requires marking as conflict.

Management Plan
- management_plan_main_or_not_recorded:
  - Arrange face-to-face appointment for full neurological exam, fundoscopy, and blood pressure measurement (booked via support team per clinician).
  - Prescribe a stronger analgesic as discussed by clinician (medication name not documented; dose/route/frequency not documented). Advise take with food. Patient may take paracetamol concurrently (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Safety net: advise urgent A&E if headache worsens, changes character, becomes unbearable, or new focal neurological signs develop.
  - If migraine with aura is confirmed on assessment, reassess suitability of combined oral contraceptive and consider alternative contraception.
  - If examination reveals red flags (focal neurological signs, papilledema, significant change in consciousness, worsening despite treatment), arrange urgent neuroimaging (e.g., CT head ± CT venogram or MRI/MRV) and consider hospital referral to evaluate for CVST, SAH, or other secondary causes.
  - If fundoscopy shows papilledema or visual loss, expedite neuroimaging and neurology/opthalmology referral.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine (probable migraine with visual aura) — High likelihood
  - Rationale: Photophobia, visual phenomena, severe disabling headache, partial response to analgesia, positive family history; no fever or focal deficits.
- Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — Moderate likelihood
  - Rationale: Combined oral contraceptive use increases thrombotic risk; subacute severe headache with visual symptoms and intermittent positional/stabbing element. Requires exclusion if exam or symptoms worsen.
- Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — Moderate likelihood
  - Rationale: Young woman with persistent headache and visual symptoms; fundoscopy needed to assess for papilledema. Lack of obesity data and absent classic features reduce likelihood but do not exclude.
